cases.sentence: Эти слова в ___ ясно показали Пьеру, что французы будут в Москве.
cases.explain: «первый раз» — after the preposition «в», the accusative marks the direct object of the verb.
cases.translation: The first declared that the report that Count Rostopchín had forbidden people to leave Moscow was false; on the contrary he was glad that ladies and tradesmen’s wives were leaving the city. “There will be less panic and less gossip,” ran the broadsheet “but I will stake my life on it that that scoundrel will not enter Moscow.” These words showed Pierre clearly for the first time that the French would enter Moscow. The second broadsheet stated that our headquarters were at Vyázma, that Count Wittgenstein had defeated the French, but that as many of the inhabitants of Moscow wished to be armed, weapons were ready for them at the arsenal: sabers, pistols, and muskets which could be had at a low price. The tone of the proclamation was not as jocose as in the former Chigírin talks. Pierre pondered over these broadsheets. Evidently the terrible storm cloud he had desired with the whole strength of his soul but which yet aroused involuntary horror in him was drawing near.

cases.sentence: — Он не успел решить, что̀ значит, как за дверью кабинета послышался голос ___, спрашивающей, можно ли войти.
cases.explain: «старшей княжны» — the genitive here marks possession, absence, or quantity.
cases.translation: “If this patience comes out,” he said to himself after shuffling the cards, holding them in his hand, and lifting his head, “if it comes out, it means … what does it mean?” He had not decided what it should mean when he heard the voice of the eldest princess at the door asking whether she might come in.

cases.sentence: (Одна ___, с длинною талией и окаменелым лицом, продолжала жить в доме Пьера; две меньшие вышли замуж.)
cases.explain: «старшая княжна» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: Only the eldest princess, the one with the stony face and long waist, was still living in Pierre’s house. The two younger ones had both married.

cases.sentence: Разве не он писал в этих ___, что какой бы там ни был, тащи его за хохол на съезжую (и как глупо)!
cases.explain: «дурацких афишах» — after the preposition «в», for location or topic.
cases.translation: “Oh, that count of yours!” said the princess malevolently. “He is a hypocrite, a rascal who has himself roused the people to riot. Didn’t he write in those idiotic broadsheets that anyone, ‘whoever it might be, should be dragged to the lockup by his hair’?

cases.sentence: В этот день Пьер, для того чтобы развлечься, поехал в село Воронцово смотреть большой ___, который строился Леппихом для погибели врага, и пробный шар, который должен был быть пущен завтра.
cases.explain: «воздушный шар» — the accusative marks the direct object of the verb.
cases.translation: To distract his thoughts he drove that day to the village of Vorontsóvo to see the great balloon Leppich was constructing to destroy the foe, and a trial balloon that was to go up next day. The balloon was not yet ready, but Pierre learned that it was being constructed by the Emperor’s desire. The Emperor had written to Count Rostopchín as follows:

cases.sentence: Внушите, пожалуста, Леппиху, чтоб он обратил хорошенько внимание на то место, где он спустится в ___, чтобы не ошибиться и не попасть в руки врага.
cases.explain: «первый раз» — after the preposition «в», the accusative marks the direct object of the verb.
cases.translation: Please impress upon Leppich to be very careful where he descends for the first time, that he may not make a mistake and fall into the enemy’s hands. It is essential for him to combine his movements with those of the commander in chief. On his way home from Vorontsóvo, as he was passing the Bolótnoe Place Pierre, seeing a large crowd round the Lóbnoe Place, stopped and got out of his trap. A French cook accused of being a spy was being flogged. The flogging was only just over, and the executioner was releasing from the flogging bench a stout man with red whiskers, in blue stockings and a green jacket, who was moaning piteously. Another criminal, thin and pale, stood near. Judging by their faces they were both Frenchmen. With a frightened and suffering look resembling that on the thin Frenchman’s face, Pierre pushed his way in through the crowd.

cases.sentence: Но вниманье толпы, — чиновников, мещан, купцов, мужиков, женщин в салопах и шубках, — так было жадно сосредоточено на то, что̀ происходило на ___, что никто не отвечал ему.
cases.explain: «Лобном месте» — after the preposition «на», for location or topic.
cases.translation: “What is it? Who is it? What is it for?” he kept asking. But the attention of the crowd—officials, burghers, shopkeepers, peasants, and women in cloaks and in pelisses—was so eagerly centered on what was passing in Lóbnoe Place that no one answered him. The stout man rose, frowned, shrugged his shoulders, and evidently trying to appear firm began to pull on his jacket without looking about him, but suddenly his lips trembled and he began to cry, in the way full-blooded grown-up men cry, though angry with himself for doing so. In the crowd people began talking loudly, to stifle their feelings of pity as it seemed to Pierre.

cases.sentence: — Что́, мусью, видно ___ кисел французу пришелся... оскомину набил, — сказал сморщенный приказный, стоявший подле Пьера, в то время как француз заплакал.
cases.explain: «русский соус» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: “Eh, mounseer, Russian sauce seems to be sour to a Frenchman … sets his teeth on edge!” said a wrinkled clerk who was standing behind Pierre, when the Frenchman began to cry. The clerk glanced round, evidently hoping that his joke would be appreciated. Some people began to laugh, others continued to watch in dismay the executioner who was undressing the other man.

cases.sentence: Приехав домой, Пьер отдал приказание своему всё знающему, всё умеющему, известному всей Москве, кучеру Евстафьевичу о том, что он в ночь едет в Можайск к войску, и чтобы туда были высланы его ___.
cases.explain: «верховые лошади» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: On reaching home Pierre gave orders to Evstáfey—his head coachman who knew everything, could do anything, and was known to all Moscow—that he would leave that night for the army at Mozháysk, and that his saddle horses should be sent there. This could not all be arranged that day, so on Evstáfey’s representation Pierre had to put off his departure till next day to allow time for the relay horses to be sent on in advance.

cases.sentence: Всё это не могло быть сделано в тот же день, и потому, по представлению Евстафьевича, Пьер должен был отложить свой отъезд до ___, с тем чтобы дать время подставам выехать на дорогу.

cases.sentence: 24-го числа прояснело после ___, и в этот день после обеда Пьер выехал из Москвы.
cases.explain: «дурной погоды» — after the preposition «после», the genitive here marks possession, absence, or quantity.
cases.translation: On the twenty-fourth the weather cleared up after a spell of rain, and after dinner Pierre left Moscow. When changing horses that night in Perkhúshkovo, he learned that there had been a great battle that evening.

cases.sentence: Все дома Можайска были заняты постоем войск, и на ___, на котором Пьера встретили его берейтор и кучер, в горницах не было места: всё было полно офицерами.
cases.explain: «постоялом дворе» — after the preposition «на», for location or topic.
cases.translation: Every house in Mozháysk had soldiers quartered in it, and at the hostel where Pierre was met by his groom and coachman there was no room to be had. It was full of officers.

cases.sentence: Казаки, пешие, ___, фуры, ящики, пушки виднелись со всех сторон.
cases.explain: «конные солдаты» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: Everywhere in Mozháysk and beyond it, troops were stationed or on the march. Cossacks, foot and horse soldiers, wagons, caissons, and cannon were everywhere. Pierre pushed forward as fast as he could, and the farther he left Moscow behind and the deeper he plunged into that sea of troops the more was he overcome by restless agitation and a new and joyful feeling he had not experienced before. It was a feeling akin to what he had felt at the Slobóda Palace during the Emperor’s visit—a sense of the necessity of undertaking something and sacrificing something. He now experienced a glad consciousness that everything that constitutes men’s happiness—the comforts of life, wealth, even life itself—is rubbish it is pleasant to throw away, compared with something … With what? Pierre could not say, and he did not try to determine for whom and for what he felt such particular delight in sacrificing everything. He was not occupied with the question of what to sacrifice for; the fact of sacrificing in itself afforded him a new and joyous sensation.
